sections.h: Job's last words: the third round, the wisdom poem and the oath (Job 22–31)
sections.b: In the third round Eliphaz accuses Job of crimes against the poor (Job 22:6–9). Job does not answer the charges but longs to find God's courtroom (23:3–7) and asks why God keeps no court days for the oppressed (24:1–12). The round then breaks down: Bildad speaks five verses (25), Zophar never speaks, and Job's words in 24:18–24 and 27:13–23 sound like his friends'. After the poem on wisdom (28), Job makes his closing defense: his former honor as judge and protector of the poor (29), his present shame (30), and his oath of innocence, which he signs and sets before God (31:35). "Here Job's words come to an end" (31:40).

common: Job's oath in chapter 31 is widely seen as the high point of Old Testament ethics.
uncommon: Some scholars read Job's closing defense (29–31) as having once led straight to God's answer from the storm (38:1), with Elihu's speeches added later.

sections.b:
Job 28 is the Bible's great poem on the search for wisdom. Humans can dig mines to the ends of the darkness and bring hidden gems to light (28:1–11), but wisdom cannot be found in the land of the living, in the Deep or the Sea, and no gold can buy it; even Abaddon and Death have only heard a rumor of it (28:12–22). God alone knows its place, because he saw it and set it in place at creation (28:23–27). To humans he says: "the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to keep away from evil, that is understanding" (28:28), the very words that describe Job in 1:1.

Unlike Proverbs 8, Sirach 24 and Baruch 3:9–4:4, Job 28 does not picture wisdom as a woman who comes to live among people. Scholars debate whether the poem is Job's speech or the narrator's interlude (see the chapter 28 page).

common: Job 28:28 is read as the same motto as Proverbs 1:7: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
uncommon: Some scholars think 28:28 was added later, because it gives humans a practical wisdom that the rest of the poem says no one can find.

sections.h: The third round of Job: the friends' doctrine breaks down
sections.b: In Job 22 Eliphaz carries the doctrine of reward and punishment to its limit: since Job suffers, he must have sinned, and so Eliphaz names sins Job never committed (22:6–9). Job answers that the wicked prosper and God sets no day of judgment (24:1–12). Then the debate breaks down: Bildad's last speech is five verses (25), Zophar never speaks, and in 24:18–24 and 27:13–23 Job seems to describe the doom of the wicked in his friends' own words. Scholars explain this as a damaged text, as Job quoting his friends, or as a deliberate collapse of the friends' argument. Either way, the book shows strict retribution failing to account for an innocent sufferer, and God later says the friends did not speak rightly (42:7).

common: The friends' view, that suffering always shows sin, is the view the book of Job was written to question.
uncommon: Some readers think Job himself never stops believing in retribution; that is why his own suffering seems to him a contradiction in God.

sections.b: Eliphaz accuses Job of the classic crimes against the poor: taking pledges, stripping the naked, refusing bread and water, sending widows away (Job 22:6–9). Job's answer in chapters 29 and 31 is the Bible's fullest portrait of a just man's care for the poor: he rescued them when they cried out, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the needy, shared his bread with the fatherless and warmed the naked with his sheep's wool (29:12–17; 31:16–20). In Job 24 he also gives one of the Bible's most detailed pictures of rural poverty: people pushed off the road, foraging in the desert, harvesting other men's fields hungry and treading winepresses thirsty (24:2–12).

sections.h: Job at the gate, and Job against God's silence
sections.b: Job was a judge in the town gate who looked into the cases of strangers and broke the jaws of the wrongdoer (Job 29:7–17), and he swears he never used his "backing in the gate" against the fatherless (31:21). Yet he charges God with keeping no court days for the oppressed (24:1, 12) and with taking away his own right (27:2). Much of Job's language is the language of a lawsuit: a case set out, pleas, an acquittal (23:4–7), an oath, a signature and a demand for the written charge (31:35–37).

Eliphaz says Job sent widows away with nothing (Job 22:9). Job says the wicked take the widow's ox in pledge (24:3) and prey on her (24:21), while he made the widow's heart sing (29:13) and never let her eyes grow dim (31:16), guiding her all his life (31:18). The pairing of widow and fatherless follows the law's concern (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 24:17).

Job is a man of Uz who never mentions Sinai, yet his oath of innocence (Job 31) touches several of the Ten Words: no other gods (31:26–28; Exodus 20:3), no adultery (31:9–12; Exodus 20:14), no lies or deceit (31:5; Exodus 20:16), no craving a neighbor's wife (31:1, 9; Exodus 20:17). His oath reaches past acts to the eye and the heart, much as Jesus does in Matthew 5:27–28.

sections.h: A gentile who keeps the spirit of the Torah
sections.b: Job 31 matches law after law of Exodus 20–23, Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24: honest scales (31:6; Leviticus 19:36), justice for slaves (31:13; Exodus 21:26–27), care for the widow, the fatherless and the poor man's coat (31:16–20; Deuteronomy 24:13, 17), fairness in court (31:21; Exodus 23:6; Leviticus 19:15), help for an enemy (31:29; Exodus 23:4–5), love for the foreigner (31:32; Leviticus 19:34) and prompt wages (31:39; Deuteronomy 24:15). Yet Job never cites a law. The chapter 31 page sets the site's wording of those laws beside each oath. Scholars debate whether the poet built the oath from the Torah or whether both share a wider ancient ethic.

sections.h: One Maker for master and slave
sections.b: Job swears he heard the complaints of his male and female slaves, and gives a reason no ancient law code gives: "Did not one Maker shape us both in the womb?" (Job 31:15). Israel's law limited a master's power (Exodus 21:20, 26–27) and gave slaves the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10), but it did not give a slave a right to bring a case against his master. Job goes further, grounding a slave's rights in creation. The argument was later used by Christian writers such as Gregory of Nyssa against slavery itself.

Job swears that no foreigner passed the night in the street, for he opened his doors onto the road, and that his household boasted no one left his table hungry (Job 31:31–32). The rabbis compared him to Abraham: Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 7) says Job's house had doors on all four sides, yet that he fell short of Abraham, who went out looking for guests.

sections.h: Kissing a hand to the sun and moon
sections.b: Among Job's oaths is a denial of secret star worship: he never looked at the sun or the moon in its glory and let his heart be led astray, or sent a kiss from his hand to them (Job 31:26–27). That, he says, would have denied the God above (31:28). Placed just after his oath that he never trusted in gold (31:24–25), it suggests that wealth and the heavenly bodies were twin temptations. Deuteronomy forbids the same worship (Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3).

sections.h: Rahab and the fleeing serpent in Job 26
sections.b: Job's hymn to God's power says that by his skill he struck Rahab down, and his hand ran through the fleeing snake (Job 26:12–13). The phrase "fleeing serpent" (nachash bariach) is the same as in Isaiah 27:1, where it names Leviathan, and as in the Ugaritic Baal myth, where Lotan the serpent is defeated. The Old Greek turns it into "the rebellious dragon." Many scholars assign the hymn to Bildad's lost speech; either way, it prepares for God's own description of Leviathan (Job 41).

In Job, Sheol swallows sinners as summer heat takes up the melted snow (Job 24:19). It lies naked before God, and there is no cover over Abaddon (26:6). Death is "the house where all the living meet," to which God will bring Job back (30:23). The shades (Rephaim) writhe below the waters (26:5).
In Job, Abaddon ("Destruction") is a name for the underworld: it lies open before God (Job 26:6), it has only heard a rumor of wisdom (28:22), and adultery is a fire that eats down to it (31:12).

Job 28 lists the treasures of the ancient world, gold of Ophir, carnelian, the sky-blue sappir, glass, coral, crystal, pearls and the topaz of Cush, to say that none can buy wisdom (Job 28:15–19). The Hebrew gem names are uncertain; sappir is probably lapis lazuli rather than sapphire.

Job's oath of innocence (Job 31) has parallels in Egypt and Mesopotamia. In chapter 125 of the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the dead person denies a long list of sins before Osiris and 42 judges. The Babylonian Shurpu incantations list sins from which a sufferer asks release. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, the righteous Danel judges the widow and the orphan at the gate, as Job did (Job 29:7–17). Job's oath shares the form but differs: it is sworn in life, to one God, as a demand for an answer.

Job swears "by the life of God, who has stripped me of my right" that he will not give up his integrity (Job 27:2–6), and in chapter 31 he binds himself with a chain of self-curses: if I did this, may that happen to me (31:7–10, 21–22, 38–40). In ancient courts such an oath could clear an accused person when there were no witnesses (Exodus 22:10–11). Job signs his oath and demands that God answer (31:35).

sections.h: No joy at an enemy's ruin
sections.b: Job swears that he never rejoiced at the ruin of someone who hated him or called down a curse on his life (Job 31:29–30). The oath reaches the hidden feelings that Leviticus 19:17–18 forbids ("Do not hate your brother in your heart") and anticipates Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:43–44).

Job's argument for the rights of his slaves rests on their shared creation: the one who made him in the belly made them too (Job 31:15). The text does not use the words "image of God," but it draws the same conclusion that Genesis 1:26–27 supports: every human being, slave or master, has the same dignity before the Creator.

sections.h: Satam: Job says God holds a grudge
sections.b: Job accuses God: "with your strong hand you bear me a grudge" (Job 30:21; compare 16:9). The verb satam is close in sound and sense to satan, "accuse, oppose," the root of ha-satan, the Accuser of the prologue (1:6). Readers who know the heavenly scene see the irony: Job blames God for the hostility the Accuser began.

Job swears he never hid his wrongs ke'adam, "as Adam did" or "as people do" (Job 31:33). If it means Adam, it recalls Adam hiding among the trees and blaming the woman (Genesis 3:8–12); Job, by contrast, would walk up to God like a prince and give an account of every step (31:37).

Job's hymn in chapter 26 pictures God spreading the north over the void, hanging the earth on nothing, tying the waters up in clouds and drawing the horizon on the face of the waters (Job 26:7–10). In Job 28 God gives the wind its weight, measures the waters, and gives the rain its law and a road for the thundercloud (the same words as 38:25), and in doing so he sees and sets wisdom (28:25–27). Both passages prepare for God's speech from the storm (38).

Two Ketiv-Qere cases in Job 30 change the sense. In 30:11 the written text reads "his cord," the reading tradition "my cord": God has slackened Job's bowstring or tent cord. The Plain English Translation follows the reading tradition, which is itself the Masoretic reading, so it does not depart from the Masoretic Text. In 30:22 the reading tradition has tushiyyah, "success" (KJV "substance"), while the written consonants point to teshu'ah, "the crash" of a storm, which the Plain English Translation and most modern versions follow.

Job 30 has the shape of a lament psalm: mocking enemies (30:1–15), a body in pain (30:16–19, 27–30), a God who does not answer (30:20–23). It ends with the harp turned to mourning (30:31) and no turn to praise.

sections.h: The guilty rescued by clean hands
sections.b: Eliphaz promises that if Job repents, his clean hands will rescue even a guilty man (Job 22:30). The words come true against Eliphaz himself: God tells him that Job will pray for the friends, and God accepts Job's prayer (42:7–9).
